text: Lesson 15 covered the Request and Requested Item tables. This lesson is about what actually drives a Requested Item from submitted to done — the fulfillment workflow built in Flow Designer.

Every Requested Item carries its own real state model: Open, for just submitted and not yet picked up. Work in Progress, while someone or something is actively fulfilling it. Closed Complete, once fulfillment finishes successfully. And Closed Incomplete or Cancelled, when the work is abandoned, rejected, or withdrawn.

Some fulfillment genuinely needs a person — racking a physical server, walking a new hire through badge pickup. For that, the right flow design creates a task for the fulfiller, waits for them to mark it complete, and only then moves the Requested Item to Closed Complete.

Other fulfillment is fully mechanical. An access-request item is the clearest case: once approved, the flow calls a REST step against the identity-provisioning system. The implementation detail that matters is waiting for a real success response before closing the item — never flipping to Closed Complete just because a request was sent. A failed response should route to Work in Progress with a note, or to Closed Incomplete if the request itself was invalid.

The most common real-world failure isn't a broken flow — it's a Requested Item stalling in Work in Progress because a fulfiller forgot about it, or an external system the REST step depends on is unreachable. Pairing the fulfillment flow with the item's own SLA means a notification fires as the breach approaches, catching the stall before the requester has to ask where their order is.
Open, Work in Progress, Closed Complete — moved by a person, or by a flow checking a real response. Next, the lab: designing fulfillment for a real catalog item from checkout to close.
